findings.title: HTTP-level failures are reported as cited DOIs that do not exist
findings.detail: doi_exists() returns ok only when Crossref answers 200 or the doi.org HEAD returns a 3xx. Only httpx.HTTPError is treated as 'network trouble is not evidence' (line 130). A 429 that is still there after _polite_get's 4 attempts, a 5xx from Crossref, or a 403/429/503 from doi.org's Cloudflare front all fall through to `return d, False`. The DOI then lands in `bad` and produces the scored integrity finding refs.bad_doi, which says it is a sign of AI-generated references (lines 166-171).
findings.failure_scenario: Crossref's public pool is under load and returns 503 for /works/{d}. The HEAD to doi.org is then rate-limited with 429. All 40 checked DOIs are reported as 'cited DOI(s) do not exist' (severity medium once 3 or more), and the paper's risk score rises because the network was busy.
findings.fix: Use three states. Crossref 200 or a doi.org 3xx means exists. A doi.org 404 (or Crossref 404 together with a doi.org 404) means missing. Anything else (429, 5xx, 403, timeout) means unknown: leave it out of `bad` and count it in stats['unchecked']. Honour Retry-After, and note 'N DOIs could not be checked' instead of flagging them.

verdict.reason: The mechanism is real, but the reviewer overstated its impact. In engine/paperinspector/refcheck.py:122-135, doi_exists() returns (d, True) only if Crossref answers 200 or the doi.org HEAD (with follow_redirects=False) returns 301/302/303/307/308. Only httpx.HTTPError is caught as "network trouble is not evidence". Any other status ends in `return d, r.status_code in (...)`, which is False: a Crossref 5xx, a 429 still there after _polite_get's 4 tries (lines 75-82), and then a doi.org 403, 429 or 503 (a Cloudflare challenge, a corporate proxy block, a rate limit). Those DOIs go into `bad`, which becomes the finding "N cited DOI(s) do not exist" (lines 166-171): severity medium at 3 or more, confidence 0.7, and it suggests the references were made by an AI tool. The path is reachable. `missing` holds every DOI OpenAlex did not return, and _openalex_batch.one() (lines 54-68) returns None on any non-200 or HTTPError. So an OpenAlex outage puts up to 40 DOIs into the Crossref/doi.org check. The web UI repeats the miscount in PaperTab.tsx:54 ("Could not be found" includes bad_dois). The part that is wrong: refs.bad_doi is not scored. It is not in models.INTEGRITY (models.py:131-138; the scored references checks are refs.nonexistent, refs.sneaked and refs.citation_pushing). Finding.kind is computed from that set (models.py:113-114, 145-146), and risk_score uses only integrity findings (models.py:156, 166). So the risk score does not rise. The real harm is a false quality note, at medium severity, accusing the paper of nonexistent or AI-fabricated DOIs. The trigger also needs two failures in a row (Crossref not 200 AND doi.org neither 3xx nor an exception). That is less common than the reviewer implies, but realistic behind proxies or under rate limits.
verdict.corrected_fix: In refcheck.py doi_exists(), return three states. Crossref 200 or a doi.org 3xx means exists. Only a doi.org 404 means missing (Crossref 404 alone is not enough, since DataCite and other registrars' DOIs are not in Crossref). Anything else (403, 429, 5xx, or HTTPError) means unknown. Leave unknown DOIs out of `bad` and record them as stats['unchecked']. Add a note such as "N DOIs could not be checked (service unavailable)" in place of the bad_doi finding. Optionally honour Retry-After on the doi.org HEAD and send the request with a browser UA to avoid Cloudflare 403s. In PaperTab.tsx:54, show unchecked DOIs separately from the bad and unmatched count. No change to risk scoring is needed, because refs.bad_doi is a quality note and not in INTEGRITY.

findings.title: DOIs are put into URLs unencoded, so '#', '?', '<' and '>' truncate them and valid references are flagged as fabricated
findings.detail: `f"https://api.crossref.org/works/{d}"`, `f"https://doi.org/{d}"` (line 127) and `f"https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:{v}"` (line 55) interpolate the raw DOI. Verified with httpx 0.28.1: for '10.1002/(sici)1097-4636(199706)35:4<492::aid-jbm9>3.0.co;2-#' the request path becomes '/works/10.1002/(sici)...3.0.co;2-' because '#' starts a fragment. Old Wiley SICI DOIs are common in reference lists and end in '#' or contain ';<>'. fetch.py has the same pattern at lines 195, 201 and 489, and history.py builds OpenAlex/NCBI URLs the same way.
findings.failure_scenario: A 2010 paper cites several 1990s Wiley articles with SICI DOIs. OpenAlex and Crossref get truncated DOIs and return 404. doi.org returns 404 for the truncated string. Each one is reported in refs.bad_doi as 'resolve nowhere ... a sign of references produced by an AI tool'.
findings.fix: Build these URLs with urllib.parse.quote(doi, safe='/()') (or quote(doi, safe='/')). For doi.org use `https://doi.org/` + quote(doi, safe='/'). Apply this in fetch._metadata, fetch._biorxiv, refcheck.one/doi_exists and history. Add a test with a SICI DOI ending in '#'.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed it from the code and with live requests. In engine/paperinspector/refcheck.py, line 55 builds the OpenAlex URL f"https://api.openalex.org/works/{'doi:' + v ...}", line 124 builds f"https://api.crossref.org/works/{d}" and line 127 builds f"https://doi.org/{d}". All three put the raw lowercased Crossref reference DOI into the URL. With httpx 0.28.1, a SICI DOI ending in '#' loses its last character because '#' starts a fragment. The request path ends in '...3.0.co;2-' for all three URLs.

One part of the report is wrong: '<' and '>' do not truncate anything. httpx percent-encodes them correctly (%3C and %3E). Only '#' (and '?', which would turn into a query string) actually causes the failure.

Live check with the real DOI 10.1002/(sici)1097-0258(19980130)17:2<239::aid-sim670>3.0.co;2-#, found through a Crossref query for 1998 Statistics in Medicine papers:
- Raw URLs: Crossref /works returns 404, doi.org HEAD returns 404, OpenAlex doi: returns 404.
- After urllib.parse.quote(d, safe='/()'): Crossref returns 200, doi.org returns 301, OpenAlex returns 200.

So the DOI is missing from `known` in OpenAlex, then fails both checks in doi_exists, gets added to `bad`, and is reported as refs.bad_doi ("resolve nowhere ... produced by an AI tool"). With 3 or more such references the severity becomes medium. The same raw pattern appears in fetch.py at lines 195 and 201 (cl.json for Crossref and OpenAlex metadata), line 489 (bioRxiv), line 243 (landing fallback) and line 522. In fetch.py it only matters for an input DOI that contains '#' or '?', which is rare for the paper being screened, so the realistic impact is in refcheck.
verdict.corrected_fix: In refcheck.py, import urllib.parse and add a helper `_q = lambda d: urllib.parse.quote(d, safe='/()')` (this encodes '#', '?', ';', '<', '>', ':' and keeps '/' and parentheses; verified working against all three services). Use `f"https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:{_q(v)}"` at line 55 (only when key == 'doi'), `"https://api.crossref.org/works/" + _q(d)` at line 124 and `"https://doi.org/" + _q(d)` at line 127. Apply the same helper in fetch.py at lines 195, 201, 243, 489 and 522 (anywhere b.doi goes into a URL path), and in history.py wherever a DOI is put into an OpenAlex or NCBI URL path. Do not change the `known`/`missing` comparison, which uses unquoted lowercase DOIs. Add a unit test that mocks httpx (respx or MockTransport) and asserts that the request path for '10.1002/(sici)1097-0258(19980130)17:2<239::aid-sim670>3.0.co;2-#' ends in '%23' and that the reference is not reported in bad_dois.

findings.title: References that could not be looked up are counted as 'not found in Crossref' (fabricated-citation signal)
findings.detail: _crossref_lookup returns None on any network error, on a non-200 status, or when _polite_get gives up after 4 attempts and returns the final 429. find() treats None as 'no match' and returns the text (line 150-151), so the reference is added to `unmatched`. Two or more unmatched references give refs.unverified with severity up to medium and wording about fabricated citations (lines 172-178).
findings.failure_scenario: The user is offline partway through, or Crossref throttles the 60 sequential bibliographic queries. Every DOI-less reference comes back None, and the report says '23 references could not be found in Crossref - fabricated citations look exactly like this'.
findings.fix: Make _crossref_lookup tell 'no result' (200 with empty items) apart from 'lookup failed' (exception or non-200), for example by returning a sentinel or raising. Count only true no-result cases as unmatched, record failures in stats['unchecked'], and skip the finding when more than a small fraction of lookups failed.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this from the code, with one correction to the description: the finding is a quality note and does not change the risk score.

**How a failed lookup becomes "not found".** In engine/paperinspector/refcheck.py:
- Lines 85-92: `_crossref_lookup` returns None in three cases. One is a successful 200 response with no items. The other two are lookup failures: any non-200 status (line 89 maps it to `[]`), and an `httpx.HTTPError` or `ValueError` exception (lines 91-92).
- Lines 75-82: `_polite_get` gives up after 4 attempts that all return 429 and hands back the final 429 response. `_crossref_lookup` then turns that into None.
- Lines 149-151: `find()` returns the reference text whenever the hit is None. Lines 167-170 add that text to `unmatched`.
- Lines 172-178: two or more unmatched references produce `refs.unverified`. Severity is low, or medium at 4 or more. The wording says "No published work matches these references" and "fabricated citations ... look exactly like this".

**Why the scenario is realistic.** The DOI-less lookups run one at a time (`ThreadPoolExecutor(1)`) over up to 60 references, so sustained Crossref throttling is plausible. A dropped connection mid-run raises `httpx.ConnectError`, which is caught and becomes None. Crossref 5xx errors and timeouts follow the same path. The pipeline only checks `online` once, before the run starts (pipeline.py:376), so losing the connection partway through is not detected. The same file already handles the DOI check differently: `doi_exists` (lines 129-130) returns True with the comment "network trouble is not evidence". The free-text path has no equivalent guard, so the gap is clearly unintended.

**Correction.** `refs.unverified` is not in the `INTEGRITY` set (models.py:131-138). It is a quality note and does not affect `risk_score`. The user-visible failure is still as described: a medium-severity note that suggests fabricated citations, caused entirely by network trouble or throttling.
verdict.corrected_fix: Have `_crossref_lookup` return three distinct outcomes. A hit returns the dict. A 200 response with an empty `items` list returns None ("no match"). An exception or any non-200 status, including the final 429 from `_polite_get`, returns a sentinel such as `FAILED = object()`, or raises. In `find()`, when the lookup returns `FAILED`, return a marker instead of the text and count it in a separate `unchecked` list. Record `stats['unchecked'] = len(unchecked)`. Emit `refs.unverified` only when lookups mostly succeeded, for example when `unchecked <= 0.2 * attempted`. When some lookups failed, mention in the detail that N references could not be checked because of network or rate-limit errors.

findings.title: Concurrent scans of the same DOI or file share the cache folder and the run id, and _new_run deletes the other job's run
findings.detail: The run id is the current second plus a hash of the DOI (line 338), or of the file in run_id_for (line 40). _new_run() runs shutil.rmtree(run) when the folder exists (lines 312-313). fetch() also gives every job for a DOI the same cache folder root/sha1(doi)[:12] (fetch.py:162-166), and _Client.download opens dest with 'wb' directly. server._job starts a thread per request with no lock or dedup.
findings.failure_scenario: The user double-clicks 'Scan', or the web app and the Mac app both submit the same DOI within a second. Job B rmtree's the run folder that job A is writing figures/evidence into, and A crashes with FileNotFoundError or writes a report that points at missing PNGs. Meanwhile both jobs write pmc/PMCxxx.pdf at the same time and corrupt it. For uploads, two identical uploads in the same second collide the same way.
findings.fix: Make run ids unique (add uuid4().hex[:6], or use mkdir(exist_ok=False) and retry with a suffix) and never rmtree an existing run. In the server, dedupe in-flight jobs by DOI or file hash and return the existing job. Guard the per-DOI cache folder with a lock (a threading.Lock dict plus an fcntl lock file), and download to a temp name in the same folder followed by os.replace.

verdict.reason:
I read the cited code, and the race is real. It is narrower than the report says.

- **Run ids can collide.** `scan_doi` (pipeline.py:338) builds the run id from `strftime('%Y%m%d-%H%M%S')` plus `sha1(doi)[:8]`. `run_id_for` (pipeline.py:35-40) builds it from the timestamp plus a hash of the file content. So two jobs for the same DOI, or for byte-identical uploads, get the same id if they reach that line in the same wall-clock second.
- **The second job deletes the first one's run.** `_new_run` (pipeline.py:311-316) calls `shutil.rmtree(run)` when the folder already exists. Job B then wipes job A's figures, evidence and `source.pdf` while A is still writing them.
- **Nothing stops two identical jobs.** `server._job` (server.py:34-54) starts a bare `threading.Thread` for each request, with no lock and no check for a matching job already running. `/api/scan` and `/api/doi` call it directly (server.py:81-97).
- **Uploads can share an id.** Each upload is saved to its own temp folder (`_save_upload` uses `mkdtemp`), but the run id is a hash of the content. Two identical uploads started within one second get the same run folder.
- **DOI jobs always share a cache folder.** `fetch.fetch` (fetch.py:~160-166) uses `root/sha1(doi)[:12]` for every job on that DOI. `_Client.download` (fetch.py:96-111) opens `dest` with `'wb'` and streams straight into it, with no temp file and no `os.replace`. Two concurrent fetches of one DOI therefore truncate and interleave writes to the same PDF, XML and supplement files. When one download fails, its `dest.unlink` can also delete the file the other job just finished. This part happens whenever two fetches of one DOI overlap, whichever second their run ids fall in.

Limits on the reported scenario:

- **The web app has a partial double-click guard.** App.tsx:59/112/118/139 disables the button and drop zone once `busy`. That only covers the gap after the job response arrives. Realistic triggers are two clients (web and Mac app, or two tabs), or a double submit before `setJob` resolves.
- **DOI run-id collisions are less likely than claimed.** `rid` is computed after `fetch()` returns, so both jobs' network fetches must finish within the same second.
- **Not every write crashes.** A's later `cv2.imwrite` calls fail silently, returning False rather than raising. Other writes into `evidence/` would raise FileNotFoundError, or the report ends up pointing at missing PNGs, as described.

Each step of the failure can be reached with realistic concurrent input; the reviewer overstates how easy it is to trigger.
verdict.corrected_fix:
1. **Unique run ids.** In `run_id_for` and `scan_doi`, append `uuid.uuid4().hex[:6]` to the run id. In `_new_run`, create the folder with `run.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=False)` and never `rmtree` an existing run. Keep the rmtree only for an explicit caller-supplied `run_dir`, if anything relies on that.
2. **Lock the per-DOI cache.** In `fetch.fetch`, hold a per-key lock for the whole fetch: a module-level `threading.Lock` per key, plus `fcntl.flock` on `b.dir/'.lock'` so separate processes (such as the CLI) are covered too.
3. **Atomic downloads.** In `_Client.download`, stream to `dest.with_name(dest.name + f'.{uuid4().hex[:6]}.part')`, then `os.replace(tmp, dest)`. On error, unlink only the temp file.
4. **Optional server dedup.** In `server._job`, take a key (the normalized DOI, or the sha1 of the uploaded file). If a running job in `JOBS` has the same kind and key, return it instead of starting a new one.

findings.title: Re-used cache folder supplies stale and partial files: the oldest PMC XML wins and leftovers become 'supplements'
findings.detail: The cache folder persists between fetches, and nothing is reused intelligently: every route downloads again, while old files stay. _pmc_package takes `next(iter(sorted(pmc.glob('*.xml'))))`, so once PMCnnn.1.xml and PMCnnn.2.xml are both present the older version 1 wins. The fallback loop at lines 348-353 iterates every file in pmc/, including files from earlier fetches and partial files left by a killed process (download writes in place, so a crash leaves a truncated file). These are added as supplements. Europe PMC and the publisher page also write into a persistent supplements/ folder.
findings.failure_scenario: A paper is scanned, then PMC publishes a corrected version 2 and the user re-scans. The XML from version 1 (old figure legends, possibly before a correction) is analysed, and the media files of both versions are listed as supplements, which creates duplicate-image findings between v1 and v2 copies of the same figure.
findings.fix: Either start each fetch in a fresh folder (rmtree the cache key folder, under the per-DOI lock) or treat the cache as a real cache: store the manifest/version in bundle.json and reuse it only when the version matches. Pick the XML/PDF by the manifest's exact names (f"{v}.xml"), not by glob. Only consider files downloaded in this fetch (track a set of written paths).

verdict.reason:
The main claim holds, but part of the failure scenario is overstated.

**Confirmed.**
- The cache folder is never cleared. `pipeline.scan_doi` (pipeline.py:337) calls `fetch.fetch(doi, HOME/"cache")`. `fetch()` (fetch.py:159-165) reuses `root/sha1(doi)[:12]` with `mkdir(exist_ok=True)` and deletes nothing. `_pmc_package` also only calls `pmc.mkdir(exist_ok=True)` (line 324).
- The oldest XML wins. PMC Cloud keys look like `PMCnnn.<ver>/PMCnnn.<ver>.xml`, and the local name is the last path segment (line 333). So after a v1 scan and a v2 rescan, pmc/ holds both `PMCnnn.1.xml` and `PMCnnn.2.xml`. `next(iter(sorted(pmc.glob('*.xml'))))` (line 339) is a lexicographic sort, so it picks `.1.xml`. Version 10 would also sort before version 2.
- The PDF is still chosen by the exact name `f"{v}.pdf"` (line 343). The run therefore pairs the v2 PDF with the v1 JATS. Figure captions, supplement labels and the XML used for text, table and reference checks all come from the stale version.
- Leftover files are picked up. The fallback loop (lines 347-353) walks every file in pmc/, including files from earlier fetches. Any `*.sNNN.*`, xlsx/csv/docx/zip file that is no longer in the current manifest still becomes a supplement. A file left half-written by a killed process is also kept. `download()` writes to `dest` in place and only removes it on HTTP or IO errors (lines 96-111), so a process kill leaves a truncated file. If this fetch does not overwrite it (for example, the new manifest no longer lists it, or the GET fails), the loop adds it.

**Overstated.**
- "Duplicate-image findings between v1 and v2 copies of the same figure" is unlikely. PMC media names (e.g. `*.g001.jpg`) normally carry no version, so the v2 download simply overwrites the v1 file.
- Figure images (`.gNNN.jpg`) are excluded from the fallback loop by its regex and suffix filter.
- Figures enter only through `_from_jats`, which maps XML hrefs to file names.
- The supplements/ folder is not globbed. Europe PMC (`_unzip`) and the publisher page (`_landing`) add only files written in this fetch, so leftovers there are inert.

The real impact is therefore a stale or mismatched XML for a re-scanned paper that PMC has re-versioned, plus stale or truncated PMC supplements. It is not duplicate figures.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In `_pmc_package` (fetch.py:323-353):
1. Start each fetch from an empty pmc/ folder: `shutil.rmtree(pmc, ignore_errors=True); pmc.mkdir()`.
2. Pick the XML by the manifest's exact name instead of by glob: `xml = pmc / _safe_name(http(man["xml_url"]).rsplit("/",1)[-1]) if man.get("xml_url") else None`, and use it only if it exists.
3. Collect the paths that `cl.download` actually returned during this call into a `written` set. Run the fallback loop over `sorted(written)` instead of `pmc.iterdir()`.
4. Optionally, make `_Client.download` write to `dest.with_suffix(dest.suffix + '.part')` and then `os.replace` it onto `dest`, so a killed process never leaves a truncated file under a real name.

findings.title: Metadata lookups never retry and report transient errors as 'no record'; a missed retraction notice gives a false clean result
findings.detail: _Client.json returns None for any non-200 or exception, with no retry on 429/5xx and no Retry-After handling. _metadata then logs 'Crossref: no record (the DOI may be wrong...)'. The `updates:` query that finds retractions and corrections (line 203) fails silently, and meta['references'] ends up empty so the whole reference check is skipped. No mailto is sent (UA at line 33 has none), so requests go to Crossref's slower public pool rather than the polite pool, which makes 429/503 more likely.
findings.failure_scenario: Crossref returns 503 for the works query during a busy period. The run finishes with no title, no references and no retraction notices. reporting.record(meta) sees no notices, so a retracted paper is not flagged and the verdict can read 'Nothing notable found'.
findings.fix: Add a small retry with backoff for 429/5xx/timeouts in _Client.json (honour Retry-After). Tell 'HTTP 404' apart from 'failed' in the log and in meta (for example meta['lookup_errors']). Add `mailto` (a configurable contact) to the UA or as a param for Crossref and OpenAlex. When the notices query fails, emit an info finding saying the retraction status could not be checked.

verdict.reason:
The core defect is real, though the reviewer overstates how bad the outcome is.

What the code confirms:
- engine/paperinspector/fetch.py:79-86: `_Client.json` returns None for any non-200 response or exception. It never retries and ignores Retry-After.
- fetch.py:33: the UA has no mailto, so requests go to Crossref's public pool, not the polite pool.
- fetch.py:195-200: a 503, 429 or timeout on the works query is logged as "Crossref: no record (the DOI may be wrong...)". A transient failure therefore looks the same as a missing DOI.
- fetch.py:203: the `updates:` notices query fails silently (`or {}`), so `notices=[]` and nothing records that the check failed.
- The same module already handles this elsewhere: refcheck.py:74-82 (`_polite_get`) backs off on 429 and honours retry-after, and refcheck.py:55-69 retries 429 for OpenAlex. fetch.py has neither.

Where the reviewer overstates it:
1. Retraction is not determined only by the notices query. reporting.py:118 also flags when `meta['is_retracted']`, which comes from the separate OpenAlex call (fetch.py:201, 233). A retracted paper slips through only if the Crossref `updates:` query fails and OpenAlex also misses it (OpenAlex is down, or doesn't mark it). Expressions of concern and corrections come only from `notices` (reporting.py:124-133), so those are lost whenever the updates query fails.
2. The reference check is not always skipped. refcheck.analyse (refcheck.py:104-108) still runs on OpenAlex `referenced_works` when Crossref `references` is empty. It is skipped only if both lookups fail.

Conclusion: a busy-period 503 or 429 can drop correction and concern notices without any warning. If OpenAlex also fails, it drops the retraction flag and the reference check too, and the verdict can fall back to "Nothing notable found" (models.py:173). The bug is real and reachable, with somewhat smaller blast radius than claimed.
verdict.corrected_fix: In `_Client.json` (fetch.py:79), retry about 3 times with backoff on 429, 5xx and httpx timeout/transport errors, honouring Retry-After as refcheck._polite_get already does. Return a status or raise so the caller can tell 404 from 'failed'. Add a configurable mailto (UA `mailto:` or a `mailto=` param) for Crossref and OpenAlex. In `_metadata`, log "Crossref: lookup failed (HTTP 503 / timeout)" instead of "no record", and record failures in `meta['lookup_errors']` (works, updates, openalex). In reporting.record, emit an info or low finding when the `updates` lookup failed ('retraction/correction status could not be checked'), so the verdict is not 'Nothing notable found' with no caveat. Do the same in refcheck.analyse when both references and referenced_works are missing because of lookup errors.

findings.title: Supplement archives are read into memory without a size limit, and a corrupt zip aborts the whole fetch
findings.detail: _Client.get() uses c.get(), which buffers the whole response and ignores MAX_FILE. That covers the Europe PMC supplementaryFiles zip (line 396, timeout 180 s per read, so effectively unbounded) and each PLOS supplement (line 467). _unzip passes the bytes to zipfile.ZipFile and z.read() without catching zipfile.BadZipFile, zlib.error or EOFError. A truncated or corrupt archive that starts with 'PK' raises out of fetch(), past the `finally`, and scan_doi fails. _landing has the same problem (is_zipfile passes, then a member read fails at line 559).
findings.failure_scenario: Europe PMC streams a 3 GB supplementary zip for a genomics paper: the engine process balloons in RAM and may be killed. Or the connection drops after 40 MB: the content starts with 'PK', ZipFile raises BadZipFile, and the user's DOI job ends with 'Bad magic number for central directory' instead of a report.
findings.fix: Route these through download() (streamed to disk with the MAX_FILE cap) and open the zip from the file. Wrap _unzip in try/except (BadZipFile, zlib.error, EOFError, OSError), log 'archive unreadable', and keep going. Also cap the total extracted bytes.

verdict.reason:
The bug is real. I confirmed it from the code, with one correction to the reviewer's failure scenario.

1) No size cap. `_Client.get()` (engine/paperinspector/fetch.py:88-94) calls `self.c.get(...)`. That reads the whole response body into memory and never checks `MAX_FILE` (150 MB, line 38). Only `download()` (lines 96-111) streams to disk with the cap. Three paths use the uncapped `get()`:
- `_europepmc` at line 396 fetches `{pmcid}/supplementaryFiles` with `timeout=180`. That is a per-read timeout, so a slow but steady stream is never cut off. The whole archive sits in `r.content` and is then wrapped in a `BytesIO` in `_unzip` (line 406).
- `_plos` at line 467 does the same for each PLOS supplement, then `dest.write_bytes(r.content)`.
- `_landing` at line 522 does the same for the landing HTML.

So a multi-GB Europe PMC supplementary archive is held fully in RAM. This path is reachable: it runs whenever a PMCID exists and the PMC S3 package gave no XML (lines 168-172).

2) Corrupt archives are not caught. `_unzip` (lines 404-416) calls `zipfile.ZipFile(...)` and `z.read(info)` with no try/except. The only guard before it is `r.content[:2] == b"PK"` (line 397). A bad central directory raises `BadZipFile`. A CRC mismatch also raises `BadZipFile`, and corrupt deflate data raises `zlib.error`. The `try/finally` in `fetch()` (lines 166-188) has no except, so the error propagates and `b.save()` is skipped. `pipeline.scan_doi` (pipeline.py:337) does not catch it either, so the DOI job fails with no report.

`_landing` has the same problem. `zipfile.is_zipfile(p)` at line 558 only checks for the end-of-central-directory record, so a member that fails to read at line 559 / `_unzip` still raises out of `fetch()`.

Correction to the scenario: "connection drops after 40 MB" usually does not produce a truncated zip. When a Content-Length is declared, httpx raises `RemoteProtocolError`, which is an `httpx.HTTPError`. Line 93 catches it and returns None. Truncation only gets through when the server sends no length (the body is delimited by closing the connection). Even so, the failure mode stands, because a zip that is corrupt or unreadable as served still kills the whole job. The memory problem stands as described.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In `_europepmc` (around line 396), replace `cl.get` with `p = cl.download(url, b.dir / "europepmc_supp.zip")`. `download()` needs a timeout parameter so it can pass 180 s. Then call `_unzip(b, p, "Europe PMC")` with the path, so `ZipFile` opens the file on disk instead of bytes in memory. Delete the zip afterwards.

In `_landing`, pass the path `p` instead of `p.read_bytes()`.

In `_plos` (around line 467), stream each supplement with `c.stream` under the `MAX_FILE` cap. Read the name from the content-disposition header on the streamed response. Do not use `get()` + `r.content`.

Change `_unzip` to take a path. Wrap the whole body in `try: ... except (zipfile.BadZipFile, zlib.error, EOFError, OSError, NotImplementedError): b.log.append(f"{source}: archive unreadable")` and return the count so far. Extract each member with `z.open(info)` + `shutil.copyfileobj` to a file instead of `z.read`. Also keep a running total of extracted bytes and stop when it passes a cap (for example 1 GB). That limits disk use and zip bombs, since `info.file_size` comes from the archive and can be false.

As a backstop, wrap the per-source steps in `fetch()` (`_europepmc`, `_plos`, `_landing`) in a per-step try/except that logs and continues. That way one bad source cannot abort the bundle, and `b.save()` still runs.

findings.title: An unexpected exception in the online checks throws away the whole scan after image analysis has finished
findings.detail: refcheck.analyse and history.check are called without try/except. Several non-HTTPError exceptions escape them: r.json() in refcheck._openalex_batch.one (line 65) raises ValueError on a non-JSON 200 body, inside ThreadPoolExecutor.map, so it re-raises. float(r.headers['retry-after']) at refcheck.py:81 raises ValueError for an HTTP-date Retry-After, and doi_exists catches only httpx.HTTPError. httpx.InvalidURL is not a subclass of httpx.HTTPError (verified: issubclass(httpx.InvalidURL, httpx.HTTPError) is False) and is raised for DOIs containing control characters such as '\t'.
findings.failure_scenario: After 4 minutes of image analysis on a 12-figure paper, OpenAlex returns an HTML maintenance page with status 200. ValueError propagates, the job ends with status 'error', and no report.json is written.
findings.fix: Wrap each online step in pipeline._analyse in try/except Exception and record the failure in extra['notes'] or an info finding ('Reference check failed: ...'). In refcheck, catch ValueError around r.json(), parse Retry-After defensively, and catch httpx.InvalidURL alongside HTTPError.

verdict.reason:
The bug is real. I reproduced it with the project venv and an httpx MockTransport. At engine/paperinspector/pipeline.py:376-381, refcheck.analyse(meta) and history.check(meta, paper) run without any try/except. In refcheck._openalex_batch.one (refcheck.py:59-65), only httpx.HTTPError is caught around cl.get, and r.json() at line 65 is unguarded. ThreadPoolExecutor.map at line 72 re-raises the worker's exception in the caller. With a 200 response carrying an HTML body, refcheck.analyse({'references':[{'DOI':'10.1/abc'}]}) raised JSONDecodeError, which is a ValueError.

The exception propagates out of _analyse before _finish (pipeline.py:403) writes the report. server.py:48-50 then catches it and sets job['status']='error', so all the earlier image analysis is lost.

The secondary paths are also confirmed:
- doi_exists (refcheck.py:122-130) catches only httpx.HTTPError. It calls _polite_get, which does float(r.headers.get('retry-after')) at line 81 and raises ValueError on an HTTP-date value.
- A URL containing '\t' raises httpx.InvalidURL. I checked that it is not a subclass of httpx.HTTPError.
- _crossref_lookup (line 91) does catch ValueError, so the Retry-After crash only reaches the pipeline through doi_exists.

history.py itself guards r.json() with (HTTPError, ValueError) at lines 85, 122 and 147. The main crash source is refcheck. Realistic triggers include a non-JSON 200 from OpenAlex, such as a maintenance page, a proxy or a captive portal. These are uncommon but plausible, and the cost is the loss of a long scan.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In pipeline._analyse, wrap refcheck.analyse and history.check separately in try/except Exception. On failure, set the matching ref_stats or history_info to {'error': str(e)}, append a note to log, and optionally add an info Finding such as 'Reference check could not finish'. The report is then still written. In refcheck.py, add the following:
- In _openalex_batch.one, wrap r.json() in try/except ValueError and return None.
- In _polite_get, parse Retry-After defensively, e.g. try float(...) except (TypeError, ValueError): use 1+attempt, and cap the sleep.
- In doi_exists, catch (httpx.HTTPError, httpx.InvalidURL, ValueError).
- Optionally, strip or validate DOIs (remove whitespace and control characters) before building URLs.

findings.title: DOI normalisation keeps URL query strings, bioRxiv version suffixes and '.full', and rejects percent-encoded DOIs
findings.detail: DOI_RE = r"10\.\d{4,9}/\S+" takes everything up to the next whitespace, and only '.,;)' is stripped. Verified results: 'https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0123456&type=printable' gives '10.1371/journal.pone.0123456&type=printable'. 'https://www.biorxiv.org/content/10.1101/2020.01.01.123456v2.full' gives '10.1101/2020.01.01.123456v2.full'. 'https://doi.org/10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0123456' gives a ValueError. The rstrip also removes a legitimate trailing ')'. The wrong DOI is also used for the cache key and the run id.
findings.failure_scenario: A user pastes a bioRxiv link from the browser bar. Crossref, OpenAlex and the bioRxiv API all 404, _biorxiv builds '...123456v2.fullv1.full.pdf', and the report comes back empty with 'Nothing notable found'.
findings.fix: First urllib.parse.unquote the input. If it is a URL, use the path or the 'id'/'doi' query param. Cut at [?&#] when the input came from a URL. Strip a trailing /v\d+(\.full(\.pdf)?)?$ for the 10.1101 prefix, and strip '.full', '.pdf' and '/full' suffixes. Strip ')' only when the parentheses are unbalanced. Add unit tests for these inputs.

verdict.reason:
This is a real bug. engine/paperinspector/fetch.py:41-49 uses DOI_RE = r"10\.\d{4,9}/\S+" and only does rstrip(".,;)").lower(). I ran normalize() on the cited inputs and got exactly what the reviewer reported:
- The PLOS URL gives '10.1371/journal.pone.0123456&type=printable'.
- The bioRxiv URL gives '10.1101/2020.01.01.123456v2.full'.
- 'https://doi.org/10.1371%2Fjournal.pone.0123456' raises ValueError, so server.py:101 returns HTTP 400.

Realistic users will hit this, because the UI asks for links. The web input is labelled "DOI or article link" with the placeholder "... or https://doi.org/…" (web/src/App.tsx:109-111), and the Mac TextField has the same placeholder (mac/Sources/PaperInspector/App.swift:156). Both send the raw string to /api/doi, which calls normalize (server.py:101). fetch() calls normalize again (fetch.py:161), and the wrong DOI then feeds the sha1 cache key/folder (fetch.py:162-163), Crossref, OpenAlex, the bioRxiv API and doi.org.

One detail of the failure scenario is wrong. When the bioRxiv API returns an empty collection, _biorxiv (fetch.py:487-503) just runs `continue`, so it never builds the '...v2.fullv1.full.pdf' URL. The real result is that every source lookup misses and the paper is not fetched. The rstrip(')') issue is also real (a DOI ending in ')' loses it), but it is rare. The main bug stands.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In normalize(), do these in order:
1. Strip the input and urllib.parse.unquote it.
2. If it parses as an http(s) URL, look for a DOI in the 'doi' or 'id' query parameter first, then in the path. Do not search the raw string, so the query and fragment are never included.
3. After matching, cut at the first [?#&] or whitespace.
4. For the 10.1101 prefix, strip a trailing r'v\d+(\.full(\.pdf|-text)?)?$' and a trailing '.full'.
5. For all DOIs, strip trailing '/full', '/pdf', '.full', '.pdf' and '/abstract'.
6. Strip a trailing ')' only when the DOI has more ')' than '('. Keep stripping '.,;' as now.
7. Lowercase the result.

Add unit tests in tests/ for: the PLOS ?id=...&type= URL, a biorxiv v2.full URL, a %2F-encoded doi.org URL, a doi: prefix, a DOI wrapped in parentheses, and a DOI with balanced parentheses (SICI style).

findings.title: OpenAI-compatible agent loop crashes on malformed tool arguments, tool errors or a malformed submit_review
findings.detail: Unlike the Anthropic path (lines 241-246), _openai has no try/except. A model emitting invalid JSON arguments (json.loads at line 279, common with local Ollama/LM Studio models) or a tool raising (for example figure_img returning None for a missing PNG, then cv2/numpy errors in _png or panel_img) ends the whole investigation. The tools are not sent with strict mode, and investigate() indexes v['finding_id'], v['verdict'] and v['reason'] (lines 304-308) without validation. A verdict missing a key, or `verdicts` returned as a string or dict, raises KeyError/TypeError after all turns have been paid for.
findings.failure_scenario: qwen2.5vl:7b on Ollama returns arguments '{finding_id: "003"}' (unquoted key). JSONDecodeError propagates and the job shows 'AI investigator stopped: Expecting property name...'. Or the model submits verdicts=[{"id":"003","verdict":"likely"}] and investigate raises KeyError: 'finding_id'.
findings.fix: Wrap json.loads and run_tool per call. On failure, append a {'role':'tool', 'tool_call_id':..., 'content':'Error: ...'} message so the model can retry. Validate submit_review args (with jsonschema, or by filtering verdicts that are dicts with the required keys and an allowed verdict value, and coercing observations), and use .get() in investigate(). Consider passing `strict: true` in the function definitions for providers that support it.

verdict.reason:
Confirmed from engine/paperinspector/agent.py. In _openai (lines 255-292), every step of the tool loop runs without a guard. Line 279 is `args = json.loads(c.function.arguments or "{}")` and line 282 is `blocks = run_tool(ws, c.function.name, args)`. Neither has a try/except. The Anthropic path does catch tool exceptions (lines 241-246) and sends its tools with "strict": True (line 214). The OpenAI tools (lines 258-260) are built with no strict flag, so nothing makes the provider follow the schema.

A local Ollama or LM Studio model that emits malformed JSON arguments therefore raises JSONDecodeError out of _openai and investigate(). server.py:251 runs it through _job, so the whole investigation fails with that error. Any exception inside run_tool (cv2 or imgdup work on odd panels, a missing figure PNG giving None) also ends the run instead of being returned to the model.

The submit_review result is returned unvalidated (line 281). investigate() then indexes v["finding_id"] at line 304 and v["verdict"] / v["reason"] at line 308. A verdict missing a key raises KeyError. If `verdicts` is a string, iterating it gives characters and `"x"["finding_id"]` raises TypeError. Either failure comes after all the paid turns, and report.json is not written.

The figure_img=None path is less likely, because the pipeline writes the figure PNGs. The malformed-JSON and malformed-verdict paths are realistic with weaker OpenAI-compatible models. The failure matches the description.

findings.title: Agent history keeps every base64 PNG for up to 24 turns, so long reviews hit request-size and image-count limits
findings.detail: Each view_evidence/view_figure/view_panel/compare_panels result adds full-resolution PNGs (up to 1400 px, often 1-4 MB of base64 each for micrographs) to `messages`, and they are never pruned. The full history is resent on every turn. The Anthropic Messages API caps a request at 32 MB, and per-request image limits apply. The OpenAI path likewise appends up to 6 images per turn as user messages (lines 286-289).
findings.failure_scenario: A paper with many duplicate candidates: the model views evidence for 8 findings (2-3 images each) and a few figures. Around turn 10 the request exceeds 32 MB or the image limit, the API returns 413/400, and the investigation fails with no review saved.
findings.fix: Encode images as JPEG (quality about 85) with a smaller max side for figures. Keep only the images from the last N tool results and replace older image blocks with a text placeholder ('[image omitted: evidence for 003]'), or use the context-editing beta (clear_tool_uses) on the Anthropic path. Cap the total images per request and save partial results on failure.

verdict.reason:
The claim holds. In engine/paperinspector/agent.py, `_anthropic` (lines 214-251) appends every tool_result to `messages` (line 250). Those results include the base64 PNG blocks built by `run_tool`/`_png` (lines 112-118, 126), and the whole list is resent on every turn (line 223). Nothing ever prunes, downsizes or replaces older images. `_openai` (lines 254-292) does the same: line 289 adds up to 6 data-URI PNGs per turn as a user message, and these also stay in the history.

I measured `_png` output with the repo's venv on figures from real runs in ~/.paperinspector/runs. Evidence pair and diff images are small, about 0.03-0.47 MB of base64 each, because side_by_side caps their height at 300 px (evidence.py:35-46). Figures are much larger. A figure at its native ~1050 px is 1.3-1.6 MB. pdfdoc renders figures at up to 300 DPI (pdfdoc.py:22), and the same figure resized to the 1400 px cap is 2.5 MB, or 3.2 MB with mild sensor noise. A 900 px panel in the view modes comes to 1.5 MB (original), 1.9 MB (reveal), 2.5 MB (noise) and 2.2 MB (false); edges is only 0.1 MB. PNG is used for everything, never JPEG.

So the 1-4 MB figure is right for figures and panel views, but evidence images are smaller than the report says. A thorough review still adds up: about 16 evidence images (~6 MB), plus 5 figures (~12 MB), plus 8 panel views (~16 MB), gives about 34 MB. That is within the 24-turn budget, and the model is told to open panels "in other views (levels, reveal, noise)". It passes the 32 MB request limit, so the API returns 413/400. The exception escapes `investigate()` (lines 295-297) before report.json is written (line 316), so all the work is lost and no partial review is saved.

The image-count limit is less likely to be the trigger, but the size failure alone is reachable with realistic input. The failure is not certain on every paper, since smaller reviews stay under the limit. It is still a real failure with input this tool is meant for: figure-heavy papers with many candidates.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In agent.py, three changes:
1. Make `_png` produce JPEG (quality about 85, media_type "image/jpeg") for photographic content. Lower `max_side` for whole figures to about 1200 and for panels to about 1000. This cuts each payload by about 3-5x.
2. Before every `messages.create`, walk `messages` and replace image blocks in all but the last 2-3 tool_result/user messages with a text block such as "[image omitted to save space: <label>; call the tool again to re-view]". Keep a running byte budget, for example rebuild the payload whenever the total base64 size goes over ~20 MB, and cap images per request at about 40. Do the same for the OpenAI path, where the images live in user messages with image_url data URIs.
3. Wrap the turn loop so that an API error (anthropic.APIStatusError / openai.APIError) or an exhausted step budget still writes a partial `ai_review`: verdicts gathered so far, an error note, and usage. Do this instead of raising before report.json is saved. Optionally, on the Anthropic path, use the context-management `clear_tool_uses` beta instead of manual pruning.

findings.title: settings.save has a read-modify-write race on a shared temp file; a corrupt settings.json silently wipes saved keys
findings.detail: FastAPI runs the sync POST /api/settings in a thread pool, and save() takes no lock. Every caller uses the same temp path settings.tmp (line 71) opened with O_TRUNC. Two overlapping saves interleave writes into the same inode, and the second os.replace raises FileNotFoundError because the first already renamed it. Even without that, concurrent saves lose updates (both load, both write). load() swallows every exception and returns DEFAULTS, so if settings.json is ever unreadable the next save() persists DEFAULTS and every stored API key is lost. A non-dict JSON value makes `{**DEFAULTS, **s}` raise TypeError outside the try.
findings.failure_scenario: In the Settings panel the user changes the provider (which saves provider, model and base_url) and immediately toggles 'can see images' or saves a key. Two requests overlap: one returns 500, and the saved key or the provider change is lost.
findings.fix: Guard save() with a module-level threading.Lock plus an fcntl.flock on a lock file (the Mac app and CLI can also write). Use tempfile.mkstemp(dir=HOME) for a unique temp name, then os.replace. In load(), only fall back to defaults when the file is missing. On a parse error, back up the bad file (settings.json.bad) and log the problem instead of overwriting it, and require the parsed value to be a dict.

verdict.reason:
The defects are in the code, but the bug is low severity and the reviewer's scenario is not the realistic trigger.

What the code does:
- engine/paperinspector/settings.py:60-77: save() runs load(), changes the dict, then writes it out. It takes no lock.
- Line 71: every call uses the same temp path, settings.tmp, opened with O_TRUNC at line 72, then os.replace at line 75.
- server.py:297-300: POST /api/settings is a plain sync `def`, so FastAPI runs it in its thread pool. Two requests can run save() at the same time.

When overlap happens, everything the reviewer lists can follow:
- Both threads write into the same inode, so the JSON can come out mixed.
- The second os.replace raises FileNotFoundError, and that request returns 500.
- Both threads load the old state, so one update is lost.
- load() at lines 52-57 catches every exception and returns {}. If the mixed write ever reaches settings.json, the next save() writes DEFAULTS plus the patch, and every stored key is gone.
- A non-dict JSON value makes `{**DEFAULTS, **s}` raise TypeError outside the try. That only happens if someone edits the file by hand.

Where the reviewer is wrong:
- The scenario as described ("change the provider, then immediately toggle vision") is two human-speed actions. Each save takes well under a millisecond, so those requests do not overlap.
- The realistic trigger is in web/src/App.tsx (Settings panel, around lines 222-272). The model and base_url inputs save onBlur, and nothing awaits that save. If you type a model and then click the vision checkbox, the effort select, or "Save key", the blur POST and the click POST go out back to back on separate connections. They can then run save() concurrently. It is a narrow, rare race, but it can happen with ordinary use.
- No other process writes the file: grep finds no settings.json writer in mac/Sources or cli.py. Only refcheck.py:42 reads it. So a cross-process fcntl.flock is not needed. An in-process lock is enough.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In settings.py, add a module-level `_LOCK = threading.Lock()` and hold it around the whole load-change-write body of save(). This closes the in-process race. The server is the only writer, so no fcntl lock file is needed.

Replace the fixed temp path with a unique one in the same directory, with a cleanup path:
`fd, tmp = tempfile.mkstemp(dir=HOME, prefix=".settings.", suffix=".tmp")`, then `os.fchmod(fd, 0o600)`, write the JSON, flush and fsync, then `os.replace(tmp, PATH)`. On any exception, unlink tmp.

Make load() strict:
- If the file is missing (FileNotFoundError), return dict(DEFAULTS).
- If it fails to parse (JSONDecodeError or OSError), or the parsed value is not a dict, copy the file to settings.json.bad and log a warning. Then either raise from save(), so it refuses to overwrite, or have load() return the defaults with a "corrupt" marker that save() checks before writing.

Have save() call an internal load that raises on corruption, so it never writes DEFAULTS over a file it could not read.

Optionally, debounce or serialize the onBlur saves in web/src/App.tsx (for example, chain each save onto the previous request's promise) so the panel does not send overlapping POSTs.

findings.title: A DOI with no reachable PDF or figures produces a 'Nothing notable found' verdict
findings.detail: When every route fails (paywalled, publisher blocks bots, network down), scan_doi continues with main=None and no figures. _analyse then scores an empty paper and verdict() (models.py:173) returns 'Nothing notable found by the automatic checks.' The only signal that nothing was checked is a status string in sources and the log list.
findings.failure_scenario: A user pastes the DOI of a paywalled Elsevier paper. Nothing can be fetched, and the report shows risk 0 with 'Nothing notable found', which reads like a clean bill of health for a paper that was never examined.
findings.fix: If there is no PDF, no JATS figures and no supplements, either fail the job with 'No open copy found - upload the PDF' or set report['coverage'] = 'metadata only' and override the verdict ('Not screened: no full text available'). Show this prominently in both apps.

verdict.reason:
I confirmed this from the code. Nothing stops a scan when fetching finds nothing, and no step warns that the paper went unexamined.

- **The fetch never fails.** `fetch.fetch` (`engine/paperinspector/fetch.py:159-190`) only logs each failed route (PMC, Europe PMC, PLOS, bioRxiv, open-access PDF, landing page) and returns the Bundle with `pdf=None`, no figures and no supplements. Its only `raise` (line 48) is for a malformed DOI.
- **The scan continues.** `scan_doi` (`pipeline.py:333-347`) sets `main = None` and calls `sources.load`. With no PDF and no XML, `sources.load` (`sources.py:90-93`) builds `Paper(pages=[""], page_count=0)` with no figures, then `_analyse` runs as usual.
- **Every content check sees an empty paper.**
  - The image checks have no figures to look at.
  - `textcheck`, `stats` and `datacheck` get empty text and no tables.
  - `reporting.statements` returns nothing when the text is under 3000 characters (`reporting.py:205-206`). So even the "missing statement" notes don't appear, which makes the report look cleaner still.
- **Only metadata checks run:** `refcheck`, `history`, `reporting.record` and `timeline`. For an ordinary paywalled paper with no retraction notices or retracted references, these find no integrity problems.
- **The verdict reads as a pass.** `risk_score` (`models.py:149-162`) returns 0, and `verdict` (`models.py:165-173`) returns "Nothing notable found by the automatic checks." `_finish` (`pipeline.py:416-421`) writes the score and verdict with no coverage field.
- **The apps only hint at it.** The web header (`web/src/RunView.tsx:97`) shows "0 figures, 0 panels" next to the Score badge, which displays the verdict. The only explicit signal is the status line "not analysed: no open PDF found - upload it to check figures" (`sources.py:101-103`). It appears only in the Files examined list on the Paper tab (`web/src/PaperTab.tsx:77-92`) and the Mac equivalent (`RunView.swift:419`). The log list isn't displayed prominently either.

A user who pastes the DOI of a paywalled paper therefore gets risk 0 and "Nothing notable found" for a paper whose full text, figures and data were never examined. The scenario is realistic and the failure is as the reviewer described.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In `_analyse` or `_finish` (`pipeline.py`), work out the coverage: full text if a PDF, JATS XML or text of at least about 3000 characters was read, and images if `paper.figures` is non-empty. Write it to the report as `report['coverage'] = {'text': bool, 'figures': int, 'tables': int, 'supplements': int}`.

When there is neither text nor figures:
- Set the verdict to "Not screened: no open full text was found. Upload the PDF to check figures, data and text." Use a separate status such as `report['screened'] = False` so the score of 0 isn't read as a pass.
- Show a prominent banner in `web/src/RunView.tsx` and `mac/Sources/PaperInspector/RunView.swift`.
- Grey out or hide the Score badge in both apps.

When text is present but no figures were found, add a qualifier to the verdict ("Image checks not run: no figures available") instead of overriding it.

Optionally, `scan_doi` could raise a clear error ("No open copy found - upload the PDF") when there is no PDF, no XML, no figures and no supplements. Keeping a metadata-only report has an advantage, though: the retraction, reference and author-record checks still have value.

findings.title: An NCBI error payload is read as 'accession does not exist'
findings.detail: `int(r.json().get('esearchresult', {}).get('count', '0'))` defaults to 0. When E-utilities returns HTTP 200 with {'esearchresult': {'ERROR': ...}} (backend failure or invalid query) or {'error': 'API rate limit exceeded'} (sometimes sent with a 200 or 429 body), count is missing and becomes 0. The accession is then added to `missing` and produces the medium integrity finding report.accession_missing.
findings.failure_scenario: NCBI's search backend hiccups during the 12 sequential esearch calls. GSE123456, a public dataset, is reported as 'cited as where the data live, but NCBI has no public record'.
findings.fix: Treat a missing 'count', or the presence of 'ERROR'/'error' keys, as unknown (n = -1). Only flag when count is explicitly '0'. Retry once on 429/5xx, and optionally pass an NCBI api_key/email from settings.

findings.title: output_config.effort is sent to every Anthropic model, and the effort value is never validated
findings.detail: _anthropic always passes output_config={'effort': cfg['effort']}. The model field is free text in Settings (web App.tsx:240), and effort is not supported on some older models: per the current API reference it errors on Sonnet 4.5 and Haiku 4.5, and Opus 4.5 accepts only low/medium/high. settings.save accepts any 'effort' string. The fallback-beta prefix check at line 222 also routes any id starting with 'claude-fable-5' or 'claude-opus-5' to client.beta with fallbacks='default', including future or older variants that may not accept that form.
findings.failure_scenario: The user types 'claude-haiku-4-5' to save money. Every request returns 400 and the investigator stops at step 1 with an opaque BadRequestError. Or the effort is set to 'xhigh' with an Opus 4.5 model, with the same result.
findings.fix: Keep an allow-list of model ids or families that support effort (and their allowed levels) and fallbacks, and omit the parameters otherwise. Validate effort against {'low','medium','high','xhigh','max'} in settings.save. Catch anthropic.BadRequestError and surface the API message.

findings.title: No overall deadline on downloads or reference checks: one slow server can hold a job indefinitely
findings.detail: httpx's timeout=30 applies per connect or read, not to the whole transfer. A server that trickles bytes can keep download() going until 150 MB arrive. In fetch, the PMC media loop has no cap on file count. refcheck runs up to 40 DOI checks plus 60 bibliographic lookups strictly in sequence (ThreadPoolExecutor(1)), each with a 30 s timeout and Retry-After sleeps, and it sends no progress updates. So the job can sit at 'Checking every reference against the literature' for tens of minutes with no feedback and no cancel.
findings.failure_scenario: A publisher's supplementary link streams at 5 KB/s. The DOI job stays at 55% for hours. With Crossref throttling, the reference check takes more than 20 minutes and looks hung.
findings.fix: Track wall-clock time in download() and abort past a per-file deadline (for example 120 s). Give fetch and refcheck total time budgets that leave the remaining work unchecked and say so. Pass progress into refcheck/history and report per-item progress. Cap the number of PMC media files.

findings.title: HTML error or login pages are saved as supplements, and zip members with the same basename overwrite each other
findings.detail: download() keeps any 200 response whatever its content-type. The publisher-page loop (line 555) and the PLOS figure loop (line 458) therefore store HTML 'access denied' or cookie-consent pages under .xlsx/.pdf/.img names, and they are listed as downloaded supplements. _unzip flattens paths with Path(info.filename).name (line 410), so 'Fig1/data.xlsx' and 'Fig2/data.xlsx' overwrite each other while n is still incremented and _add_supp dedups silently. The per-zip MAX_SUPP check also ignores supplements already collected.
findings.failure_scenario: A Wiley supplementary link answers 200 with an HTML 'cookies required' page. It is saved as 'mmc1.xlsx', sources fails to parse it, and the report lists it as a downloaded supplement that could not be read. The real data are never fetched and the user is not told the download failed.
findings.fix: Check content-type and magic bytes after downloading (%PDF, PK, image signatures, or text for csv/tsv). Delete and log files that look like HTML. When unzipping, keep a sanitised relative path or de-duplicate names with a counter, and stop at MAX_SUPP across all sources.

findings.title: An exhausted OpenAlex budget makes the citation analyses disappear without any note
findings.detail: _openalex_batch retries a 429 twice with fixed 1-2 s sleeps, ignores Retry-After, and then returns None. When the shared daily budget is used up, every lookup fails, works stays empty, and n < 8 skips the self-citation, citation-pushing, journal self-citation, off-topic and retracted-reference checks. Nothing goes into stats or notes, unlike history.py, which records a note on 429. Six worker threads also hammer the API while it is already rate-limited.
findings.failure_scenario: On a shared university network the OpenAlex budget runs out by mid-afternoon. A paper that cites 6 retracted works shows no refs.retracted finding and no hint that the check did not run.
findings.fix: Count 429s and other failures in _openalex_batch. If most lookups failed, set stats['note'] = 'OpenAlex limit reached - add a key in Settings' and show it. Honour Retry-After and back off once for all threads (a shared Event) rather than per thread.

findings.title: OpenAI-compatible path echoes provider-specific message fields and sends schema keywords some providers reject (plausible)
findings.detail: messages.append(msg.model_dump(exclude_none=True)) sends back every non-None field of the assistant message, which can include annotations=[], audio, or provider extras such as DeepSeek's reasoning_content. Some OpenAI-compatible servers reject unknown or echoed fields, and DeepSeek's reasoner rejects reasoning_content in input. The tool parameters also carry 'additionalProperties': False, which Gemini's OpenAI-compatibility layer has historically rejected in function declarations.
findings.failure_scenario: Selecting DeepSeek with model 'deepseek-reasoner', or Gemini: the second request fails with a 400 about an unexpected field, so the investigator never gets past step 2.
findings.fix: Rebuild the assistant message explicitly: {'role':'assistant', 'content': msg.content or '', 'tool_calls': [{'id', 'type':'function', 'function': {'name', 'arguments'}}]}. Strip additionalProperties (or use a per-provider schema adapter) for providers that reject it.

findings.title: An explicit 'vision' setting carries over when the provider changes
findings.detail: resolved() uses the preset's vision only while s['vision'] is None. The web UI clears model and base_url on a provider change (App.tsx:233) but not vision, and the checkbox (App.tsx:258) always saves an explicit bool. Once vision has been toggled for one provider, the stale value applies to every later provider.
findings.failure_scenario: The user unchecks 'can see images' for DeepSeek, then switches to OpenAI gpt-5. The investigator gets no view_figure/view_panel tools and the 'cannot see images' system note, and quietly gives a much weaker review.
findings.fix: Reset vision to None in save() whenever the provider changes (or have the UI send vision: null), and store vision per provider.

findings.title: CLI shows raw tracebacks for bad DOIs and network or AI failures, and the doi command cannot run offline
findings.detail: main() does not catch the ValueError from fetch.normalize, httpx errors, or the RuntimeError from investigate ('No API key...'), so the user sees a full traceback. The `doi` command always runs the online reference and record checks (pipeline.scan_doi passes online=True) and has no flag to skip them. `case` has no --json option even though the other commands do.
findings.failure_scenario: `paperinspector doi 'https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-020-2012-7'` prints a Python traceback ending in ValueError instead of a one-line message.
findings.fix: Wrap command dispatch in try/except (ValueError, RuntimeError, httpx.HTTPError), print a short message, and return exit code 2. Add a --no-online flag to `doi` (and pass it through scan_doi) and --json to `case`.
